Wayfair, 138 S.Ct. 1714 (2018) expanded the reach of state sales tax laws to apply to out-of-state businesses selling goods or services to consumers within their jurisdiction if they meet certain criteria. The decision held that states could require remote sellers to collect and remit sales tax based on where the consumer was located, rather than only requiring them to do so for transactions with physical stores. This change in federal law has had far-reaching implications for both businesses and consumers.

For online retailers, this decision means that they now have to file sales tax returns in all states where they sell products. They argued that because these customers weren't physically present in their state, they didn't owe any tax. However, under the new rules, they must now comply with state sales tax laws regardless of whether they have a physical presence in those states.

For consumers, the decision means that they may be required to pay more in state sales tax when shopping online. This can add up over time, especially for frequent shoppers who purchase items frequently across different states.

Overall, the impact of the South Dakota v. Wayfair decision is complex, affecting not just business-to-consumer transactions but also business-to-business transactions as well as international trade.
